newsitem.title: USA: Pathfinder's rover set to explore Mars.
newsitem.headline: Pathfinder's rover set to explore Mars.

text.p: The exploration of Mars was ready to enter a new stage on Sunday with the Pathfinder's roving vehicle Sojourner preparing to venture out onto the planet's surface.

The Sojourner, a solar-powered vehicle about the size of a microwave oven, rolled out of the Pathfinder lander late on Saturday and was parked in the Martian dust for the night. Scientists hope the Sojourner, which travels at a speed of one centimetre (0.3937 inches) per second, will help them analyse rocks and soil. In addition to its on-board laboratory, it is equipped with lasers that will help it navigate the Martian terrain.

Communication with Sojourner was restored on Saturday after a brief outage, much to the relief of scientists at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, who so far have enjoyed a nearly flawless mission.

"I didn't think we could top yesterday, but I certainly feel that way today," Richard Cook, the Pathfinder mission manager, told reporters late on Saturday as the six-wheeled vehicle rolled off the lander and headed for the planet's surface. "We've got some great images and all the scientists are in red heaven."

Pictures transmitted from the surface of the planet showed the high-tech Sojourner sitting about a vehicle's length away from the lander vehicle. One image taken by the rover's binocular camera showed the ramp as it drove slowly down the 35-degree slope.
A distinct track from the six-wheeled rover was visible -- the first sign of terrestrial life since the Viking missions of the 1970's took thousands of photographs.

A mission control technician spliced together several still frames of the roll-out, to produce a short movie of the rover as it took about four minutes to drive down the ramp and onto the surface of Mars.
About an hour after it came down the ramp, the entire Pathfinder system was shut down for the night as the Earth set over Mars.
A camera on the lander will begin taking high-resolution photographs of the region in order to chart the solar-powered Sojourner's exploration over the next week.
On Saturday, the successful deployment had been in doubt when National Aeronautics and Space Administration officials struggled to overcome a communications problem between the rover and the lander.

System engineer Matt Wallace, announcing the glitch had been resolved, said the specific cause of the communications problem was not clear but that it was believed to be in the software. Data indicated the lander vehicle's computer had re- set itself on Friday night and may have been awaiting further instructions from mission control.
The news ended some 12 hours of nail-biting tension at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory here as space engineers and technicians worked to salvage the $266-million Pathfinder mission.
Pathfinder crash-landed on Mars on Friday after a seven month journey of 309 million miles (497 million km) since being launched from Cape Canaveral.
The mission marks the beginning of an ambitious U.S. programme over the next decade to explore Mars and determine if it ever supported any life forms.

In addition to the Sojourner's mission, scientists on Sunday hope to see a new set of photographs from the Pathfinder lander, which was re-named after the late legendary NASA scientist and author Carl Sagan.
